name: Perfectha

lead:
Perfectha is a brand of hyaluronic acid (HA) fillers made by Sinclair. Clinicians inject them to restore volume or reshape features, and one product, Subskin, is among HA gels indicated for chin projection.
Laboratory studies have used the range to compare how gels break down and how cells respond, but no patient trials have been published.

paras: Treatment is performed by a qualified injector in a clinic. HA gels differ in stiffness, swelling and particle size, and clinicians choose products by area. Results are temporary and can be reversed with hyaluronidase.

HA fillers in general can cause bruising, swelling, infection, lumps and rarely vascular occlusion with vision loss or necrosis. Regulation varies: devices are CE-marked in the UK/EEA and FDA-approved only for specific products in the US.

angle.text: Clinicians place the gel to restore volume or enhance contour such as chin projection; the effect is temporary and adjustable.

lead: Perfectha is a line of resorbable hyaluronic acid fillers marketed by Sinclair. Products in the range differ by degradation time, linked to the size of their particulate HA components [1].

In the aesthetic context, such fillers are injected to add volume or contour. A 2026 comparison of four HA gels indicated for chin projection included Perfectha Subskin alongside Juvederm Volux and Restylane Lyft and Shaype [2].
Wikipedia describes HA fillers as biocompatible and biodegradable, usually cross-linked with BDDE for stability, with most results lasting around six months [3].

paras: Macrophage studies exposed cells to extracts of experimental HA preparations and commercial Perfectha fillers, testing whether cross-linking degree relates to adverse effects; cytotoxic responses were absent to minimal [1]. A skin-model study similarly examined foreign-body-type gene responses [4]. An in-vitro study compared how Subskin and other HA gels degrade under two hyaluronidase formulations [5]. A rheology study compared Subskin with other chin gels [2].

HA fillers generally can cause bruising, redness, pain and itching, less commonly infection or allergic reaction, and rarely vision loss from embolization or delayed necrosis [3]. Researchers note migration, late swelling and inflammation as complications whose link to product properties is not well understood [1].
In the US the FDA regulates fillers as medical devices, while in the UK/EEA they are CE-marked [3].
No studies found of Perfectha in patients among the cited sources; the research above is laboratory-based [1][2][4][5].
